restraint.author: Homer
restraint.locator: Iliad 1, Athena restrains Achilles; Book 1, normalized characters 9293-10273
restraint.excerpt: The son of Peleus was furious, and his heart within his shaggy breast was divided whether to draw his sword, push the others aside, and kill the son of Atreus, or to restrain himself and check his anger. While he was thus in two minds, and was drawing his mighty sword from its scabbard, Minerva came down from heaven (for Juno had sent her in the love she bore to them both), and seized the son of Peleus by his yellow hair, visible to him alone, for of the others no man could see her. Achilles turned in amaze, and by the fire that flashed from her eyes at once knew that she was Minerva. “Why are you here,” said he, “daughter of aegis-bearing Jove? To see the pride of Agamemnon, son of Atreus? Let me tell you—and it shall surely be—he shall pay for this insolence with his life.” And Minerva said, “I come from heaven, if you will hear me, to bid you stay your anger. Juno has sent me, who cares for both of you alike. Cease, then, this brawling, and do not draw your sword

aftermath.author: Homer
aftermath.locator: Iliad 1, Achilles appeals to Thetis; Book 1, normalized characters 17110-17588
aftermath.excerpt: Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea, weeping and looking out upon the boundless waste of waters. He raised his hands in prayer to his immortal mother, “Mother,” he cried, “you bore me doomed to live but for a little season; surely Jove, who thunders from Olympus, might have made that little glorious. It is not so. Agamemnon, son of Atreus, has done me dishonour, and has robbed me of my prize by force.” As he spoke he wept aloud, and his mother heard him

narrativeBlocks.title: Agamemnon threatens a second seizure
narrativeBlocks.body: Agamemnon says he will return Chryseis but take Briseis from Achilles as compensation. His speech makes the quarrel about public rank and control of captives.

narrativeBlocks.title: Achilles considers violence
narrativeBlocks.body: The passage says Achilles is divided between drawing his sword against Agamemnon and restraining his anger.

narrativeBlocks.title: Athena intervenes
narrativeBlocks.body: Athena tells Achilles not to draw his sword. The conflict continues through speech and a seizure of Briseis rather than becoming a duel.

narrativeBlocks.title: Achilles turns to the sea
narrativeBlocks.body: After Briseis is taken, Achilles goes alone to the shore, weeps, and calls on his mother Thetis.

narrativeBlocks.title: Honor has a public cost
narrativeBlocks.body: The poem frames a dispute between leaders as a danger to the larger Achaean host. Preserve the sequence: threat, restraint, seizure, grief.
